title: Letters about the story wheel
public_context: Two teachers at a fictional lower school exchange professional letters about a writing workshop. The correspondence sits in a teaching portfolio with diagrams and student work, and concerns the ordinary planning and reflection that accompany a classroom activity. The writers use the exchange to share classroom language across a school year.
source_title: Three letters between Aven Rowe and Lio Marr, collected in a teaching portfolio
source_text:
Dear Lio, the story wheel worked better than I expected once I stopped treating it as a race. We put six paper spokes on the table, each with a different opening condition: a locked window, a missing shadow, a late visitor, and three others the children invented. Each pair chose one spoke and wrote only the next two sentences before turning the wheel to the next pair. The new pair had to keep one detail from the page but could change the narrator. That rule gave the quieter writers a way to enter without defending the whole story.

I worried that the turn would make every plot crooked, so we read the pages aloud after the third handoff. In one story a baker's door was locked in the first section, yet a later narrator walked through it without noticing. The children caught the mismatch before I did. They decided that the baker had opened a side hatch, then added a sentence showing it. I kept the first draft under the revised one in the folder so the class could see why a small bridge mattered. No child was asked to claim a page as solely theirs; the wheel made the pages shared work.

Your reply about the red-pencil table helped. I tried it the next Friday: anyone could put a folded note beside a sentence they wanted to keep unchanged, and the group had to ask that writer before editing it. The first note protected a deliberately repeated word, not a spelling error. The group left it alone and revised the surrounding sentence instead. I did not collect the notes for marks, and nobody lost a turn for declining to read aloud. One child asked if the rule meant a writer could veto any change in the entire story. I said the note protected one marked sentence for that session, not the plot forever.

I am sending the wheel diagram and the two versions of the baker story, with the children's names removed. We have not decided whether the next workshop will use the same spokes or start with endings. The head of the lower school asked whether we could show the work at the family evening, but I have not answered because the children have not discussed that invitation. If we do share it, I would rather show the revisions than choose a winning story. Your own class may find the turn useful, though it may need fewer spokes for a shorter period.

licensed_inferences.claim: The wheel's handoff rule allowed plot continuity to be corrected by the group rather than only by the teacher.
licensed_inferences.rationale: Pairs inherited one detail and jointly supplied the side-hatch bridge, which was preserved with the earlier draft. The account does not claim that all continuity errors were caught.

licensed_inferences.claim: The protection note constrained a specific edit rather than giving a writer control over the whole shared story.
licensed_inferences.rationale: The note applied to one sentence for one session and was not used for marks. The author explicitly rejected a permanent plot veto, so the inference is limited to the described rule.
